If the infant's physical examination is normal and the serum quantitative nontreponemal serologic titer is the same or less than fourfold the maternal titer, and the mother was either untreated, inadequately treated, or has no documentation of treatment, or was treated with erythromycin or another non-penicillin regimen, or received treatment less than 4 weeks before delivery, the preferred treatment regimen is as follows: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G at 100,000–150,000 units/kg/day, administered as 50,000 units/kg/dose intravenously every 12 hours during the first 7 days of life and every 8 hours thereafter for a total of 10 days. Alternatively, procaine penicillin G at 50,000 units/kg/dose intramuscularly once daily for 10 days. If more than one day of therapy is missed, the entire course should be restarted. 2. If the infant's physical examination is normal and the serum quantitative nontreponemal serologic titer is the same or less than fourfold the maternal titer, and the mother was treated during pregnancy with appropriate therapy for the stage of infection, administered more than 4 weeks before delivery, and has no evidence of reinfection or relapse, the preferred treatment regimen is: Benzathine penicillin G at 50,000 units/kg/dose intramuscularly as a single dose. 3. If the infant's physical examination is normal and the serum quantitative nontreponemal serologic titer is the same or less than fourfold the maternal titer, and the mother’s treatment was adequate before pregnancy, with her nontreponemal serologic titer remaining low and stable before and during pregnancy and at delivery (e.g., VDRL <1:2 or RPR <1:4), no treatment is required. However, benzathine penicillin G at 50,000 units/kg intramuscularly as a single dose may be considered, particularly if follow-up is uncertain. 4. For congenital syphilis in infants and children, the preferred regimen is: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G at 50,000 units/kg intravenously every 4–6 hours for 10 days. 5. For leptospirosis, the preferred regimen is: Doxycycline 200 mg orally once a week. 6. For tick-borne relapsing fever caused by Borrelia recurrentis, the preferred regimen is: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 5–10 days. An alternative regimen is erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 5–10 days. If meningitis or encephalitis is present, ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 12 hours for 14 days is recommended. 7. For louse-borne relapsing fever, the preferred regimen is: Tetracycline 500 mg orally as a single dose. An alternative regimen is erythromycin 500 mg orally as a single dose. 8. For early Lyme disease caused by Borrelia burgdorferi: Adults with erythema migrans should be treated with: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10–21 days. Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 14–21 days. Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily for 14–21 days. Alternative regimens include azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily for 7–10 days, clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily for 14–21 days, or erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 14–21 days. Pediatric patients under 8 years of age should receive: Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses every 8 hours (maximum 500 mg per dose). Cefuroxime axetil 30 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses every 12 hours (maximum 500 mg per dose). Pediatric patients 8 years or older should receive: Doxycycline 4 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses every 12 hours (maximum 100 mg per dose). Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily (maximum 500 mg per day). Clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg orally twice daily (maximum 500 mg per dose). Erythromycin 12.5 mg/kg orally four times daily (maximum 500 mg per dose). 9. For Lyme meningitis and other early neurologic manifestations: Adults should receive ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 24 hours for 10–28 days. Alternative regimens include cefotaxime 2 g intravenously every 8 hours, penicillin G 18–24 million units intravenously every 4 hours, or doxycycline 200–400 mg/day orally in divided doses for 10–28 days. Pediatric patients should receive ceftriaxone 50–75 mg/kg intravenously once daily (maximum 2 g), cefotaxime 150–200 mg/kg/day intravenously in divided doses every 6–8 hours (maximum 6 g/day), or penicillin G 200,000–400,000 units/kg/day intravenously in divided doses every 4 hours (maximum 18–24 million units/day). Doxycycline 4–8 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses (maximum 100–200 mg per dose) may be used for children 8 years or older. 10. For Lyme carditis: The preferred regimen is ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 24 hours for 10–28 days. Patients with advanced heart block may require a temporary pacemaker, and consultation with a cardiologist is recommended. Oral antibiotic therapy should be used to complete the treatment course for outpatients, as used for erythema migrans without carditis. 11. For borrelial lymphocytoma: The same regimens used to treat erythema migrans are recommended. 12. For late Lyme disease: Lyme arthritis should be treated with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily or amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily. An alternative regimen is cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily for 28 days. Pediatric patients should receive amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses three times daily (maximum 500 mg per dose), cefuroxime axetil 30 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses twice daily (maximum 500 mg per dose), or doxycycline 4 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses twice daily (maximum 100 mg per dose) for children 8 years or older. For persistent or recurrent joint swelling after a recommended course of oral antibiotics, re-treatment with another 4-week course of oral antibiotics or a 2–4 week course of intravenous ceftriaxone is recommended. 13. For patients with arthritis and objective evidence of neurologic disease: The preferred regimen is ceftriaxone intravenously for 2–4 weeks. Alternative regimens include cefotaxime or penicillin G intravenously. Pediatric patients should receive ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or penicillin G intravenously. 14. For late neurologic Lyme disease: The preferred regimen is ceftriaxone intravenously for 2–4 weeks. Alternative regimens include cefotaxime or penicillin G intravenously. Pediatric patients should receive ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or penicillin G intravenously. 15. For acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans: The preferred regimen is doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 21 days or amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 21 days.
